sections.title: Angles in standard position
sections.locator: CNXML module m51283, section 'Drawing Angles in Standard Position'
objectives: Identify the initial side, terminal side and vertex of an angle, and describe an angle as a rotation.
Draw a positive or negative angle in standard position and name the quadrant that holds its terminal side.
Recognise quadrantal angles and state their measures.

misconceptions.claim: A negative angle is smaller than zero and therefore cannot be drawn.
misconceptions.correction: The sign records the direction of the rotation, not its size. An angle of $-135°$ is a rotation of 135° in the clockwise direction.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m51283, section 'Drawing Angles in Standard Position'

misconceptions.claim: An angle in standard position may start from any ray.
misconceptions.correction: Standard position fixes the vertex at the origin and the initial side on the positive $x$-axis. Only the terminal side moves.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m51283, section 'Drawing Angles in Standard Position'

summary: An angle in standard position has its vertex at the origin and its initial side on the positive $x$-axis.
A counterclockwise rotation is positive; a clockwise rotation is negative.
Quadrantal angles have terminal sides on an axis: 0°, 90°, 180°, 270° and 360°.

content.text: An angle is a rotation, not a shape. Fix the initial side on the positive $x$-axis, turn the terminal side through the given measure, and the drawing follows from the fraction of a full turn: $90°$ is a quarter turn, $180°$ a half turn, and $270°$ three quarters. The sign tells the direction of the turn, so a negative angle is drawn clockwise while its size stays positive. Examination questions usually ask for the quadrant or for a sketch, and both come from counting quarters rather than from measuring with a protractor.

hints: Divide the measure by 360° to see what fraction of a full turn the angle represents.
Think of the arrow near the vertex: which way is it turning?

authored_exercises.stem: Sketch an angle of $210°$ in standard position and state the quadrant in which its terminal side lies.
authored_exercises.answer: The terminal side lies in the third quadrant.
solution: Starting from the positive $x$-axis, rotate counterclockwise through $180°$ to reach the negative $x$-axis.
Rotate a further $30°$. The terminal side lies between $180°$ and $270°$, so it is in the third quadrant.
hints: Compare the measure with 180° and 270°.

authored_exercises.stem: An angle in standard position has measure $-150°$. Describe its rotation and name the quadrant of its terminal side.
authored_exercises.answer: A clockwise rotation of 150°; the terminal side lies in the third quadrant.
solution: The negative sign means the rotation is clockwise from the positive $x$-axis.
A clockwise turn of $150°$ passes the negative $y$-axis at $90°$ and stops before $180°$, so the terminal side is in the third quadrant.
hints: A negative angle turns clockwise.
Third-quadrant angles lie between 180° and 270° counterclockwise, or between 90° and 180° clockwise.

sections.title: Radian measure and degree conversion
sections.locator: CNXML module m51283, sections 'Converting Between Degrees and Radians' and 'Identifying Special Angles Measured in Radians'
objectives: Define the radian as the ratio of an arc length to the radius, and explain why it has no unit.
Convert between degrees and radians using $180°=\pi$ radians.
Recognise the common angles in both units.

misconceptions.claim: A radian is a length, measured in centimetres or inches.
misconceptions.correction: A radian is the ratio of two lengths, arc divided by radius, so the units cancel and the measure is dimensionless.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m51283, section 'Using Radians'

misconceptions.claim: $1$ radian equals $180°$.
misconceptions.correction: Half a turn is $\pi$ radians, which is $180°$, so one radian is about $57.3°$.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m51283, section 'Relating Arc Lengths to Radius'

summary: A full turn is $360°$ or $2\pi$ radians; a half turn is $180°$ or $\pi$ radians.
Multiply degrees by $\frac{\pi}{180}$ to get radians, and radians by $\frac{180}{\pi}$ to get degrees.
The special angles are $30°=\frac{\pi}{6}$, $45°=\frac{\pi}{4}$, $60°=\frac{\pi}{3}$ and $90°=\frac{\pi}{2}$.

content.text: Degrees and radians answer the same question with different units. A radian is the angle whose intercepted arc equals the radius, so a full turn is $2\pi$ radians and a half turn is $\pi$ radians. Convert by keeping the proportion $\frac{\theta}{180°}=\frac{\theta_R}{\pi}$: multiply degrees by $\frac{\pi}{180}$ to reach radians, and radians by $\frac{180}{\pi}$ to reach degrees. The special angles recur in every later section, so learn them as pairs rather than converting each time.

sections.title: Coterminal angles
sections.locator: CNXML module m51283, sections 'Finding Coterminal Angles' and 'Finding Coterminal Angles Measured in Radians'
objectives: Find an angle coterminal with a given angle by adding or subtracting full turns.
Find the least positive coterminal angle in degrees and in radians.

misconceptions.claim: Coterminal angles are equal angles.
misconceptions.correction: They share a terminal side but have different measures. $140°$ and $-220°$ are coterminal, not equal.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m51283, section 'Finding Coterminal Angles'

misconceptions.claim: To find a coterminal angle you add $180°$.
misconceptions.correction: A coterminal angle differs by a full turn: $360°$ in degrees or $2\pi$ radians. Half a turn lands on the opposite side of the circle.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m51283, section 'Finding Coterminal Angles Measured in Radians'

summary: Coterminal angles differ by whole turns: $\theta+360°k$ or $\theta+2\pi k$ for an integer $k$.
Choose $k$ so that the result lies in $0°\le\theta<360°$ or $0\le\theta<2\pi$.
Every angle has infinitely many coterminal angles.

content.text: Every angle has infinitely many coterminal partners, because adding or subtracting a full turn returns the terminal side to the same place. In degrees add or subtract $360°$; in radians add or subtract $2\pi$. Examination questions usually ask for the least positive partner, which means choosing the number of turns that lands the angle in $0°\le\theta<360°$ or $0\le\theta<2\pi$. A coterminal angle is not equal to the original, only indistinguishable on the circle.

sections.title: Arc length and sector area
sections.locator: CNXML module m51283, sections 'Relating Arc Lengths to Radius', 'Using Radians', 'Determining the Length of an Arc' and 'Finding the Area of a Sector of a Circle'
objectives: Use $s=r\theta$ to find an arc length when the angle is in radians.
Use $A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta$ to find the area of a sector.
Convert a degree measure to radians before applying either formula.

misconceptions.claim: The formulas $s=r\theta$ and $A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta$ accept an angle in degrees.
misconceptions.correction: Both formulas need $\theta$ in radians. Convert first, or the answer is wrong by a factor of $\frac{\pi}{180}$.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m51283, section 'Finding the Area of a Sector of a Circle'

misconceptions.claim: The area of a sector is $\pi r^2\theta$.
misconceptions.correction: The sector is the fraction $\frac{\theta}{2\pi}$ of the circle, so $A=\frac{\theta}{2\pi}\pi r^2=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta$.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m51283, section 'Finding the Area of a Sector of a Circle'

summary: Arc length is $s=r\theta$ when $\theta$ is in radians.
Sector area is $A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta$ when $\theta$ is in radians.
A sector is the fraction $\frac{\theta}{2\pi}$ of the whole circle.

content.text: Arc length and sector area are the two circular measures that follow directly from radian measure. When $\theta$ is in radians, an arc cuts a length $s=r\theta$ and a sector encloses an area $A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta$. The sector formula is the fraction $\frac{\theta}{2\pi}$ of the whole circle area, so it also explains why the angle must be in radians. If a question gives degrees, convert first; that one step prevents most errors.

sections.title: Linear and angular speed
sections.locator: CNXML module m51283, section 'Use Linear and Angular Speed to Describe Motion on a Circular Path'
objectives: Distinguish linear speed from angular speed on a circular path.
Compute angular speed as $\omega=\frac{\theta}{t}$ and linear speed as $v=r\omega$.
Convert between revolutions per minute and radians per unit time.

misconceptions.claim: Every point on a rotating wheel has the same linear speed.
misconceptions.correction: Every point has the same angular speed, but $v=r\omega$ grows with the radius, so a point on the rim moves faster than a point near the centre.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m51283, section 'Use Linear and Angular Speed to Describe Motion on a Circular Path'

misconceptions.claim: You can substitute revolutions per minute directly into $v=r\omega$.
misconceptions.correction: $v=r\omega$ requires $\omega$ in radians per unit time. Convert revolutions per minute to radians per minute by multiplying by $2\pi$.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m51283, section 'Use Linear and Angular Speed to Describe Motion on a Circular Path'

summary: Angular speed is $\omega=\frac{\theta}{t}$; linear speed is $v=\frac{s}{t}$.
The two are linked by $v=r\omega$ when $\omega$ is in radians per unit time.
One revolution is $2\pi$ radians, so revolutions per minute convert by $2\pi$.

content.text: Two speeds describe motion on a circle. Angular speed $\omega=\frac{\theta}{t}$ measures how fast the angle turns, while linear speed $v=\frac{s}{t}$ measures how fast a point travels along the arc. They meet in $v=r\omega$, which holds only when $\omega$ is in radians per unit time. On the same wheel every point has the same angular speed, but a point farther from the centre has the greater linear speed because it travels a longer arc in the same time.

misconceptions.claim: The sine of an angle is the adjacent side over the hypotenuse.
misconceptions.correction: Sine is opposite over hypotenuse. The adjacent side over the hypotenuse is cosine.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m51284, section 'Using Right Triangles to Evaluate Trigonometric Functions'

misconceptions.claim: The cofunction identity applies only to sine and cosine.
misconceptions.correction: Every function pairs with its cofunction at complementary angles: sine with cosine, tangent with cotangent, and secant with cosecant.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m51284, section 'Using Equal Cofunction of Complements'

summary: SohCahToa: sine is opposite over hypotenuse, cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, tangent is opposite over adjacent.
Secant, cosecant and cotangent are the reciprocals of cosine, sine and tangent.
$\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-t\right)=\cos t$, and the same pattern pairs every function with its cofunction.

content.text: Right-triangle trigonometry names six ratios of the sides, and every one of them depends on which acute angle is chosen. The three primary ratios are sine, cosine and tangent, remembered as SohCahToa; the other three are their reciprocals. Because the two acute angles of a right triangle are complementary, the sine of one is the cosine of the other, which is the cofunction identity. The special triangles supply exact values without a calculator.

misconceptions.claim: An angle of elevation is measured from the vertical.
misconceptions.correction: Angles of elevation and depression are measured from the horizontal. The line of sight is compared with a horizontal line through the observer.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m51284, section 'Using Right Triangle Trigonometry to Solve Applied Problems'

misconceptions.claim: If the known side is adjacent to the angle, use sine.
misconceptions.correction: Sine uses the opposite side. When the known side is adjacent and the unknown is opposite, use tangent; when the unknown is the hypotenuse, use cosine.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m51284, section 'Using Trigonometric Functions'

summary: Label the sketch first, then choose the ratio that names the known angle, the known side and the unknown.

content.text: Most right-triangle problems are solved by labelling the sketch before reaching for a ratio. Mark the known angle, the known side and the side you want, then choose the ratio that mentions exactly those three quantities. If the unknown is an angle, apply the inverse function at the end. Angles of elevation and depression are both measured from the horizontal, which is why a line of sight upward and a line of sight downward to the same object produce equal angles when the two horizontal lines are parallel. Round only at the final step.

sections.title: Sine and cosine on the unit circle
sections.locator: CNXML module m51285, sections 'Finding Trigonometric Functions Using the Unit Circle', 'Defining Sine and Cosine Functions from the Unit Circle', 'Finding Sines and Cosines of Angles on an Axis' and 'The Pythagorean Identity'
objectives: Define $\cos t$ and $\sin t$ as the coordinates of a point on the unit circle.

misconceptions.claim: On the unit circle, the sine of an angle is its $x$-coordinate.
misconceptions.correction: Cosine is the $x$-coordinate and sine is the $y$-coordinate: the point is $(\cos t,\sin t)$.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m51285, section 'Defining Sine and Cosine Functions from the Unit Circle'

misconceptions.claim: The Pythagorean identity gives a single value for the missing function.
misconceptions.correction: It gives two values, one positive and one negative. The quadrant of the angle decides which one is correct.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m51285, section 'The Pythagorean Identity'

summary: A point at angle $t$ on the unit circle has coordinates $(\cos t,\sin t)$.
At quadrantal angles the coordinates are read directly from the axes.
$\cos^2 t+\sin^2 t=1$, and the quadrant fixes the sign of the function being found.

content.text: The unit circle turns trigonometry into coordinates. A point at angle $t$ on the circle of radius 1 has coordinates $(\cos t,\sin t)$, so cosine reads the horizontal displacement and sine the vertical one. Substituting these coordinates into $x^2+y^2=1$ gives the Pythagorean identity $\cos^2 t+\sin^2 t=1$. The identity fixes the size of one function given the other, and the quadrant supplies the sign.

A calculator must be in the mode that matches the input, degree or radian, because the same keystrokes mean different things in the two modes. Sine and cosine accept every real angle as input and return values between $-1$ and $1$.

content.text: A reference angle is the acute angle between the terminal side and the horizontal axis. It carries the size of the trigonometric value, while the quadrant carries the sign. In quadrant II subtract the angle from $180°$, in quadrant III subtract $180°$ from the angle, and in quadrant IV subtract the angle from $360°$; the radian versions use $\pi$ and $2\pi$. The same method gives the coordinates of any point on a circle of radius $r$ through $(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)$.

content.text: Tangent, secant, cosecant and cotangent complete the set of six functions. On the unit circle, tangent is $\frac{y}{x}$ and the other three are reciprocals of cosine, sine and tangent respectively. Their signs follow the same quadrant rule: all six are positive in quadrant I, only sine and cosecant in quadrant II, only tangent and cotangent in quadrant III, and only cosine and secant in quadrant IV. A calculator without cosecant, secant or cotangent keys evaluates them as reciprocals.

misconceptions.claim: Cosine is an odd function because the cosine of a negative angle is negative.
misconceptions.correction: Cosine is even: $\cos(-t)=\cos t$. Sine is the odd one, $\sin(-t)=-\sin t$.

misconceptions.correction: Divide $\sin^2 t+\cos^2 t=1$ by $\cos^2 t$ to get $1+\tan^2 t=\sec^2 t$. The cosecant form comes from dividing by $\sin^2 t$.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m51286, section 'Alternate Forms of the Pythagorean Identity'

summary: Cosine and secant are even; sine, tangent, cosecant and cotangent are odd.
Rewriting a function as sine or cosine simplifies most expressions.
$1+\tan^2 t=\sec^2 t$ and $1+\cot^2 t=\csc^2 t$.
Sine, cosine, secant and cosecant have period $2\pi$; tangent and cotangent have period $\pi$.

content.text: Identities are equations that hold for every angle where both sides are defined, and they are the tools that turn a complicated expression into a simple one. Cosine and secant are even, so they ignore the sign of the angle; sine, tangent, cosecant and cotangent are odd, so they change sign. Dividing the Pythagorean identity by $\cos^2 t$ or $\sin^2 t$ produces the two alternate forms, $1+\tan^2 t=\sec^2 t$ and $1+\cot^2 t=\csc^2 t$. The period is $2\pi$ for sine, cosine, secant and cosecant, and $\pi$ for tangent and cotangent.
